data_section_full_text:
3. Data sources and variables


Data sources
Data for this study come from the COMPUSTAT, Center for Research in Securities
Prices (CRSP), Institutional Brokers Estimate System (I/B/E/S), and Trade and
Quote (TAQ) data bases. From COMPUSTAT, I collect data on all firms with 1995
earnings-per-share and market-value data. From CRSP, I collect the standard deviation of daily returns and daily trading volume for each month of 1995. From the
I/B/E/S summary tape, I gather three analyst characteristics: the number of analysts
supplying a one-year ahead earnings forecast in a given month ( Number ); the standard deviation of those forecasts; and the consensus (mean) forecast. From the last
two variables, I create the variable CV (the coefficient of variation of the analyst
forecasts, defined as the standard deviation scaled by the absolute value of the
mean forecast).

CAR Vol. 20 No. 3 (Fall 2003)

Analyst Following and Market Liquidity 559


By definition, calculating CV requires that sample firms be followed by at
least two analysts. As discussed in endnote 2, I require a minimum of five analysts
to conform to theoretical work and to avoid selection bias and nonlinearity issues
arising from a sample with firms that are and are not followed by analysts. Results
are not sensitive to the minimum number of analysts used.

Using observed forecasts as a proxy for analyst coverage assumes that published
forecasts capture the information-producing/disseminating activity analysts. However, it may be that analysts provide significant information even in periods in
which forecasts are not actively issued. For example, prior research has found that
forecast revisions (dispersion) increase (decreases) throughout the year as the earnings announcement draws closer, indicating that analysts may “cover” a firm but
choose not to issue forecasts until later in the firm’s fiscal year. If analysts contribute to the information environment of a firm even in months in which they do not
issue forecasts, my tests will be biased against measuring the effect of analyst
activity on liquidity. To mitigate this problem, I start the sample period in April,
thereby eliminating the months most likely to have analyst coverage without a
forecast. <sup>7</sup> Further, I have replicated my main tests with an analyst following variable that incorporates the number of forecast revisions (gathered from the I/B/E/S
detail tape), thereby giving greater weight to active analysts. Results are similar to
those presented.

To be consistent with prior research (e.g., Chung et al. 1995), I use CV as
opposed to the raw standard deviation of the forecasts. Results are similar when the
unscaled standard deviation or range of the forecasts proxies for analyst dispersion.
My tests assume that forecast dispersion is a proxy for the quality of information
about the firm. This assumption is supported by the finding in Bartov, Lynn, and
Ronen 1999 that earnings-response coefficients decrease in the level of forecast
dispersion. Forecast dispersion may also proxy for differences in how analysts process information (including the frequency with which forecasts are updated) and
for differences in private information across analysts. If true, this would call into
question my inferences about analysts being primarily public information providers
who reduce the information asymmetry faced by market makers. However, the analyst literature has found mixed results in documenting significant differences in
ability across analysts, suggesting that dispersion at least partially proxies for the
quality of information available to all analysts.

From TAQ, I collect every quoted spread and depth from a New York Stock
Exchange (NYSE) specialist and every NYSE trade for the last week of the sample
months. <sup>8</sup> The last week is chosen because I/B/E/S publishes its consensus forecast in the third week of each month. I then average the spreads and depths for
each firm, creating the variables Spread and Depth . The final sample has complete
COMPUSTAT and I/B/E/S data for approximately 10,000 firm-months. Restricting the sample to firms with December 31 fiscal year-ends, at least five analysts
